<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and stayed on the motion, but A built the tighter comparative frame. A consistently distinguished access from algorithmic amplification, and its pressure questions exposed two real gaps in B's case: B never established that incidental exposure's civic value outweighs the inflammatory content the same casual users avoid, and B never showed that a more partisan audience among recipients actually increases societal polarization rather than merely shrinking the audience. B's answers to these (especially "I don't need to prove a society-wide polarization score moved... not a claim requiring precise measurement") read as assertion rather than demonstration, and A's closing directly capitalized on this by naming the asymmetric weighing B never resolved. A also neutralized B's central "fix the ranking, not access" alternative by pointing out the two are not mutually exclusive, so it doesn't function as a genuine competing policy. B's strongest and most original material was the concrete classification-harm example (LGBTQ health info, protest organizing misclassified as "political"), which A only partially answered by calling it an implementation risk rather than a defeater — this kept B's case alive but wasn't enough to overturn A's tighter framing of the core tradeoff. Overall a close, well-matched debate, but A ends with the cleaner, more resolved path to the decision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's closing point that "CON cannot count those discoveries while assigning zero value to the inflammatory recommendations those same users avoid" (A5.3), landing on B's unanswered pressure-question response about polarization ("not a claim requiring precise measurement," B4.3), which exposed that B's structural-harm claim was asserted rather than demonstrated.</best_rebuttal>
